title: Publish your CLI tool for real
description: Publish a real package with a stated version requirement, correctly-scoped shipped files, honest semver, and an install section clear enough for someone else to follow with no help from you.

learningObjectives.text: Publish an npm package with a declared engines requirement and a files allowlist scoping what ships
Write an install section a stranger can follow start to finish with no additional context

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every filter this module covers only really proves itself the moment someone who isn't you tries to install and run the tool from nothing but what you published and what you wrote. This lab is that moment — a real publish, and a README good enough to hand to a stranger with no other explanation.

contentSections.title: Publish your CLI tool for real
contentSections.brief: Take a CLI tool of your own (from an earlier module's lab, or a new small one) to an actual, real npm publish — even a scoped, unlisted package is fine, the goal is a genuine install from the registry, not a local npm link. If publishing to npm isn't an option for you right now, a git-based install (npm install github:you/repo) is an acceptable substitute that still exercises every filter in this module except the registry-specific ones.
contentSections.deliverable: A published package a stranger installed and ran from your README alone

stages.title: State the real requirements
stages.instructions: Add an accurate engines field to package.json. Test your tool against the minimum version you declared (or the closest you can get) to confirm the requirement is actually correct, not just a guess.
stages.checkpoint: package.json declares a specific, tested Node version requirement.

stages.title: Scope what ships and choose the version bump
stages.instructions: Add a files allowlist (or a thorough .npmignore) so only what a user's install actually needs ships. Run npm pack --dry-run and review the file list. Choose your version bump (patch/minor/major) honestly based on what actually changed since the last version, not on how much code changed.
stages.checkpoint: npm pack --dry-run shows only files a real install needs, and the chosen version bump matches semver's actual compatibility promise.

stages.title: Check the cross-platform basics
stages.instructions: Search your code for hardcoded path separators or string-concatenated paths and replace them with path.join. Confirm any home-directory reference uses os.homedir(), not a literal ~. If you can, check filename casing consistency between your imports and the actual files on disk.
stages.checkpoint: No hardcoded path separators remain, and home-directory paths are built with os.homedir(), not a literal ~.

stages.title: Publish and write the install section
stages.instructions: Publish for real. Write an install section with the stated requirement, the literal command in a code block, a verify step whose output distinguishes a fresh install from a stale one, and the single most common failure with its real fix (not sudo). Have someone else — or a fresh terminal session with no prior context — follow it exactly as written.
stages.checkpoint: The tool is genuinely installable from the published package using nothing but the README's install section.

rubric.criterion: Requirements are real and tested
rubric.meets: The engines field states an actual tested requirement, not a guess or an omitted field.

rubric.criterion: Only necessary files ship
rubric.meets: npm pack --dry-run shows a scoped file list — no tests, dev notes, or example env files with real-looking values.

rubric.criterion: The version bump matches semver's actual promise
rubric.meets: The chosen bump (patch/minor/major) reflects compatibility impact, not code volume.

rubric.criterion: No hardcoded cross-platform assumptions
rubric.meets: Paths are built with path.join and os.homedir(), not string concatenation or a literal ~.

rubric.criterion: The install section is copy-pasteable, not descriptive
rubric.meets: The literal install command sits in a code block; nothing is described in prose that should be a command.

rubric.criterion: The verify step actually verifies
rubric.meets: The verify step's expected output distinguishes the newly-installed version from a stale prior install.

contentSections.body: A package that only you have ever successfully installed isn't published yet, in any way that matters — this lab is where a stranger's install either works from the README alone, or tells you exactly what still doesn't.

A single exit code is technically invalid in POSIX systems
Scripts can't read exit codes without a specific library

questions.explanation: A script deciding whether to retry, alert, or move on needs to distinguish failure categories through the exit code, since it isn't parsing human-readable error text.

questions.from: The previous module — Errors, Exit Codes and Scriptability
questions.prompt: Why is isTTY the wrong check for deciding whether to output JSON, even though it's the right check for deciding whether to emit color?

options.label: isTTY only tells you whether a terminal is directly attached, not what data shape the destination actually wants — a human piping into less is a non-TTY too
isTTY is undefined in most Node.js versions
JSON output requires a TTY to render correctly

questions.explanation: Color is safe to auto-detect because no piped destination wants raw ANSI codes; data shape is a content decision a piped human reader (via less) might still want as plain text, which isTTY alone can't distinguish.

questions.from: The previous module — Errors, Exit Codes and Scriptability
questions.prompt: For an independent-items batch job, what's the right default when one item fails?

options.label: Continue processing the rest, collect failures, report a summary, and exit nonzero if any failed
Stop the entire batch immediately at the first failure
Catch the error, log it quietly, and exit 0

questions.explanation: Independent items have no bearing on each other, so continuing preserves the work that would have succeeded — but the exit code still has to honestly reflect that something failed.

questions.from: The previous module — Errors, Exit Codes and Scriptability
questions.prompt: A CLI tool has 100% unit test coverage on its internal functions, yet a real bug shipped in how the command line calls them. What kind of test would have caught it?

options.label: A subprocess-level test that spawns the real binary and asserts on stdout, stderr and exit code
More unit tests of the same internal functions, with additional edge cases
A manual, one-time check that the command runs without crashing

questions.explanation: Unit tests never exercise argument parsing, exit-code setting, or stdout/stderr routing — only a subprocess test spawning the real binary touches that layer at all.

questions.from: Three or more modules back — Designing a CLI People Won't Fight
questions.prompt: invtrack has five distinct actions, each needing its own required arguments. What's the actual signal it needs subcommands rather than one flag-driven command?

options.label: Three or more genuinely distinct actions whose arguments don't compose with each other
The tool has more than five total flags
The author personally prefers the git-style interface

questions.explanation: curl stays a single command because its flags all tune one job. Five separate jobs with separate required arguments is the tell for subcommands — not raw flag count or stylistic preference.

questions.from: Three or more modules back — Designing a CLI People Won't Fight
questions.prompt: What should a multi-subcommand CLI, run with zero arguments, actually do?

options.label: Print the same usage summary --help shows, and exit nonzero
Exit silently with code 0
Guess the most common subcommand and run it automatically

questions.explanation: Silent exit is indistinguishable from broken, and auto-guessing hides the tool's vocabulary from exactly the person who needs to learn it.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint — that's the design, not a failure.

title: Where an AI call belongs in a fast local tool
description: Keeping an AI step out of a command's default, frequently-run path, and putting it behind an explicit subcommand or flag instead, so a 50-times-a-day command stays fast.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a tool's fast local path from an AI-dependent feature that shouldn't block it by default
Design an AI feature as an explicit, opt-in subcommand rather than folded into a frequently-run default command

contentSections.title: The command that used to be instant

contentSections.body: invtrack's `overdue` command used to return in under 100 milliseconds — read a local cache, filter, print. Someone adds a feature: each overdue invoice now gets an AI-generated one-line "likely reason for delay" summary, folded straight into the default `overdue` output. Every run of a command people ran dozens of times a day now takes four to eight seconds, waiting on a Claude API call for every single invoice in the list.

contentSections.scenario: invtrack overdue is a command run constantly, throughout the day, specifically because it used to be instant. The new AI summary adds real, occasionally very useful information — but only sometimes, and only when someone actually wants the extra context.
contentSections.question: Where does the AI summary actually belong?

options.label: Folded into overdue's default output, since more information is always better
Behind an explicit flag or a separate subcommand (e.g. --explain or invtrack explain 104), so the fast path stays fast and the AI step is something the user deliberately asks for
Removed entirely — a CLI tool with a sub-100ms reputation should never call an API at all

feedback.default-path: More information isn't free here — it's four to eight seconds of latency added to every single run of a command whose whole value, for most of the day, was being instant. The people running `overdue` twenty times a day to do a quick check now pay that cost every time, whether or not they wanted the summary.
feedback.opt-in: Right. The summary is genuinely useful sometimes, not always — an explicit flag or subcommand lets someone who wants it pay the latency cost deliberately, on the specific invoice they care about, while the fast default path stays exactly as fast as it always was for everyone else.
feedback.never: This throws away a real feature people would use, for a problem that has a much cheaper fix — the issue was never 'AI calls are bad,' it was 'the AI call was on the wrong path,' folded into a command that specifically earned its reputation by being fast.

contentSections.concept: **A network-dependent AI call has real, unavoidable latency (typically low seconds) that a local operation doesn't.** Keep it off a command's fast, frequently-run default path, and put it behind something explicit — a flag or a separate subcommand — that a user reaches for on purpose, on the specific item they want it for.

contentSections.body: Keep AI calls off a command's fast, frequently-run default path — put them behind an explicit flag or subcommand a user reaches for on purpose.

contentSections.title: The latency budget that decides the answer

contentSections.body: A different case: invtrack's brand-new `import` command already takes two or three seconds just parsing a large CSV and writing the results. Someone proposes adding an AI step that flags likely-duplicate invoices as part of that same import — and this time, nobody objects, because the two-or-three-second baseline already means users aren't expecting instant.

contentSections.scenario: The AI-summary-in-overdue case from the first half of this lesson was rejected as a default; the AI-duplicate-check-in-import case is being accepted as a default, in the very same tool.
contentSections.question: What's the actual distinction that makes one of these fine as a default path and the other not?

options.label: import's AI step is simpler code to write than overdue's would have been

import's existing baseline latency is already multiple seconds, and it runs occasionally — adding more latency to an already-multi-second, occasional operation costs far less than adding it to a near-instant, constantly-run one
There's no real distinction — one of these two decisions must be wrong

feedback.code-simplicity: Both features are roughly the same kind of code — one Claude API call per item, awaited before continuing. Implementation complexity isn't what's driving the different call here.
feedback.latency-budget: Right. The deciding factor is each command's existing latency budget and how often it's actually run. overdue was instant and run constantly — any added latency is a large relative cost paid very often. import was already multi-second and run occasionally — the same kind of added latency is a much smaller relative cost, paid rarely.
feedback.inconsistent: Both decisions are consistent with the same underlying rule — they just apply it to two commands with genuinely different existing latency profiles and usage frequency, which is exactly why the rule produces different answers for each.

contentSections.body: The actual rule isn't "AI calls are fine" or "AI calls are bad" — it's a latency budget question, asked per command: what does this command's baseline latency already look like, and how often is it run? A command that's already multi-second and occasional (import, export, a report generator) has real room to add a few more seconds of AI-step latency to its default path without changing the user's experience of it. A command that earned a reputation for being instant, run dozens of times a day (overdue, status, list), has almost no such room — any AI step there needs to be opt-in, not default.

The decision isn't about AI calls in the abstract — it's each command's existing latency budget and run frequency. A slow, occasional command has room for more latency in its default path; a fast, constant one doesn't.

title: Streaming output so the terminal doesn't feel frozen
description: Streaming a Claude response token by token instead of waiting for the whole thing, and disabling the stream (buffering the full response instead) when the destination isn't an interactive terminal.

learningObjectives.text: Use the Claude SDK's streaming API to print tokens as they arrive instead of waiting for the full response
Decide when streaming should be disabled in favor of a single buffered write

contentSections.title: Five seconds of nothing

contentSections.body: `invtrack explain 104` calls Claude, waits for the entire response, then prints it all at once. For the five-to-eight seconds that call takes, the terminal shows absolutely nothing — no cursor movement, no partial text, nothing to indicate the command is even still running. More than one user has hit Ctrl-C mid-call, assuming the tool had frozen.

contentSections.question: What's the actual problem with this code, given the Ctrl-C reports?

options.label: max_tokens is set too low for a good response
The entire response is awaited in full before anything is printed, so the terminal shows nothing at all for the full duration of the call, indistinguishable from a hang
console.log is the wrong function to print an AI response with

feedback.wrong-tokens: 150 tokens is a reasonable budget for a one-sentence response — this isn't a quality problem, and it doesn't explain why the terminal shows nothing during the wait.
feedback.no-feedback: Right. `await client.messages.create(...)` blocks until the *entire* response is generated server-side before any of it reaches the client — from the terminal's point of view, that's several seconds of complete silence, exactly the condition someone reasonably interprets as a frozen or hung process.
feedback.wrong-log: console.log correctly prints the final text once it exists — the problem is entirely about the gap in feedback before that point, not about how the eventual text gets displayed.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is switching from `messages.create()` to `messages.stream()`, which delivers tokens as they're generated rather than waiting for the whole response — the terminal shows text appearing progressively within a second or so of the call starting, the same visible-progress signal a human expects from any process that's actually working, not stuck.

contentSections.body: Stream a response so the first visible token arrives almost immediately, instead of waiting several seconds in total silence for the whole thing — that silence is what reads as a hang, not the total wait time itself.

contentSections.title: When streaming is the wrong choice

contentSections.body: A script wraps `invtrack explain 104 --json`, piping the output into a program that expects one clean JSON object on stdout. invtrack's new streaming code writes tokens to stdout as they arrive, the same as it does in an interactive terminal — the script receives a stream of partial JSON fragments, none of which parse on their own, and the pipeline breaks immediately.

contentSections.question: Put invtrack's decision logic for whether to stream in the order it should actually be checked.
steps: Check whether --json was requested at all
If --json was requested, buffer the full response and emit one complete, valid JSON object at the end — never partial fragments
If --json was not requested, check process.stdout.isTTY
If isTTY is true, stream tokens progressively for visible, human-facing progress
contentSections.explanation: The --json check comes first because it's the harder constraint: a script parsing JSON needs one complete, valid object, full stop — streaming partial fragments there isn't a style choice, it's a correctness bug, the same category of problem the CLI-design module's stdout/stderr lesson and this module's own machine-readable-output lesson both cover. Only once JSON mode is ruled out does isTTY become relevant, and there it's back to being the right tool for its actual job: deciding whether a human is watching right now and would benefit from progressive, visible output.

contentSections.body: A --json consumer needs one complete, valid object, never partial streamed fragments — buffer the full response for --json mode, and reserve progressive printing for the human-facing, non-JSON path.

title: Caching AI responses for a tool people run repeatedly
description: Caching an AI response by a hash of its real input, storing it in the tool's cache directory from the config module, and knowing when caching is actively the wrong choice.

learningObjectives.text: Design a cache key that captures everything the AI response actually depends on
Identify when a use case shouldn't cache an AI response at all, because repeated variation is the point

contentSections.title: Paying twice for the same answer

contentSections.body: A developer runs `invtrack explain 104`, reads the result, closes the terminal, and reopens it two minutes later to run the exact same command again because they wanted to re-read it. invtrack makes a fresh Claude API call, waits the same five-plus seconds, and returns the exact same answer — the invoice hasn't changed, nothing about the situation is different, and the second call was pure waste.

contentSections.scenario: invtrack explain <id> always calls Claude fresh, even for an invoice whose underlying data hasn't changed since the last time explain was run on it.
contentSections.question: What's the right fix?

options.label: Cache the response, keyed by a hash of the invoice data that actually went into the prompt, with a way to force a fresh call
Cache the response, keyed by the invoice ID alone
Don't cache at all — every AI call should always be fresh, to guarantee accuracy

feedback.cache-by-id: This looks right until the invoice's underlying data changes — a payment gets recorded, a due date is corrected — and the cache keeps serving the old, now-inaccurate explanation forever, because the ID alone hasn't changed even though the input to the prompt has.
feedback.cache-by-input-hash: Right. Hashing the actual content that goes into the prompt (the invoice's current data, plus the system prompt version, in case that changes too) means the cache is only ever a hit when nothing the answer could depend on has actually changed — and a real change automatically produces a cache miss, with no manual invalidation logic needed.
feedback.never-cache: This throws away a real, safe optimization — an unchanged invoice re-explained a minute later doesn't become *more* accurate by paying for a second identical API call; it's the same input producing the same output, just slower and more expensive the second time.

contentSections.concept: **Cache by a hash of the actual content that determines the response — not by an identifier that might stay the same while the underlying content changes.** An ID-based cache key silently serves stale answers after real data changes; a content-hash key naturally invalidates itself the moment anything the answer could depend on changes.

contentSections.body: Cache an AI response keyed by a hash of everything that determines it — the actual input content and the prompt version — so a real change naturally invalidates the cache instead of requiring manual invalidation logic.

contentSections.title: The tool where caching would be a bug

contentSections.body: A second tool, `namegen`, suggests three creative names for a new side project based on a short description. Someone reuses invtrack's caching pattern wholesale — same input, same output, every time. A user runs `namegen "a tool for tracking overdue invoices"` three times in a row hoping for three different sets of options, and gets the identical three suggestions every single time.

contentSections.scenario: namegen caches by a hash of its input description, the same pattern that worked well for invtrack explain.
contentSections.question: Why does the same caching pattern that helped invtrack actively hurt namegen?

options.label: namegen's use case depends on the model's non-determinism producing different, fresh output on each run — caching defeats the entire point of running it again
namegen's hashing function has a bug that invtrack's doesn't
Caching is never appropriate for any creative-writing use case, full stop

feedback.wrong-fit: Right. invtrack explain and namegen have opposite relationships to repetition — explain's whole value is a *stable, unchanging* answer for unchanged data, which is exactly what caching preserves. namegen's whole value, run a second time, is *new* options, which caching directly prevents by serving the exact same result every time.
feedback.hash-bug: The hash function works correctly in both cases — it faithfully reproduces the same key for the same input, which is precisely the behavior that's right for invtrack and wrong for namegen.
feedback.never-creative: The problem isn't that namegen is creative — it's that this specific use case wants a *different* answer each time it's asked, deliberately. A creative tool whose users explicitly want a stable, memorable result for the same prompt (unlikely here, but real in other cases) could still reasonably cache.

contentSections.body: The deciding question before adding a cache to any AI-backed feature: does this use case want the same answer every time for the same input, or does it want variation on purpose? invtrack's explain, a summarizer, a classifier — all want a stable, repeatable answer, and caching is a pure win. namegen, a brainstorming tool, anything explicitly offering "give me another option" — all want fresh output on each request, and caching there isn't neutral, it's actively broken. The fix for namegen isn't a smarter cache key; it's no cache at all for that endpoint, full stop.

Cache only when repeated identical output is the goal — a tool whose value depends on fresh variation each run shouldn't cache at all, no matter how well the same caching pattern worked somewhere else.

title: Falling back when the API is unavailable
description: Keeping a tool's non-AI functionality working even when the API fails, retrying transient failures but not permanent ones, and never letting an AI-feature failure take down the whole command.

learningObjectives.text: Isolate an AI feature's failure so it doesn't break the tool's non-AI functionality
Distinguish API failures worth retrying from ones that should fail immediately

contentSections.title: One failed call takes down the whole command

contentSections.body: Anthropic's API has a brief outage. invtrack's `overdue --explain` (a combined flag showing the normal list plus AI summaries) throws an uncaught exception the moment the Claude call fails, crashing before printing anything at all — including the plain, entirely-local overdue list that had nothing to do with the failed API call and was ready to print regardless.

contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw, given that the API outage is temporary and out of invtrack's control?

options.label: getOverdueInvoices() should also be wrapped in a try/catch

A failure in the optional AI-explanation step propagates up and prevents printTable() from ever running, even though the invoice list itself was already successfully loaded and has nothing to do with the failed API call
The Claude API itself is unreliable and shouldn't be used in production tools

feedback.wrong-catch-target: getOverdueInvoices() is a local, non-network operation — it isn't the thing failing here, and wrapping it changes nothing about the actual bug.
feedback.unisolated-failure: Right. The AI explanation is explicitly an optional add-on (`--explain`) layered on top of data that already loaded successfully — its failure has no logical reason to prevent the core, already-available data from being shown at all.
feedback.api-unreliable: Any external API can have transient outages — that's a fact of distributed systems, not a reason to avoid using one. The actual bug is architectural: invtrack's own code let an optional feature's failure block a core feature that didn't depend on it.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix isolates the optional step: wrap the AI call per-invoice in its own try/catch, substitute a clear fallback message on failure, and let the table print regardless. `for (const inv of invoices) { try { inv.explanation = await explainInvoice(inv); } catch { inv.explanation = '(AI explanation unavailable)'; } }` — one failed call degrades gracefully to a placeholder, and the table the user actually asked to see prints either way.

contentSections.body: The general principle: an optional, additive feature failing should never take down the core functionality it was added on top of. This is the same shape as the config module's keychain-fallback lesson — a failure in one layer (the keychain, here the AI call) degrades to a working fallback (a plaintext-with-warning path, here a placeholder message) rather than crashing the whole operation.
An optional AI feature's failure should degrade gracefully to a clear fallback message, never crash or block the core functionality it was layered on top of.

contentSections.title: Retry the blip, not the mistake

contentSections.body: invtrack's fallback handling now catches every API error, but treats them all identically — a brief network blip and a genuinely malformed request both just get logged as "(AI explanation unavailable)" with no retry at all, even for the case where trying again half a second later would very likely have worked.

contentSections.scenario: Deciding, per HTTP status code from a failed Claude API call, whether it's worth an automatic retry.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuinely worth retrying automatically? Select all that apply.

items.label: 429 — rate limited
529 — the API is temporarily overloaded
500 — an unspecified server error
401 — invalid API key
400 — malformed request (e.g. a prompt that violates the request schema)

explanation.429: A rate limit is explicitly transient — waiting (ideally with backoff) and retrying is exactly what it's asking for, and it's very likely to succeed shortly after.
explanation.529: An overloaded API is a temporary capacity issue on the provider's side — the same request very plausibly succeeds moments later once load drops, making this worth retrying.
explanation.500: An unspecified server-side error is often transient in practice — retrying with backoff is the reasonable default, even without a more specific diagnosis of the cause.
explanation.401: A bad or expired API key won't fix itself between one attempt and the next — retrying the exact same request just wastes time reproducing the identical failure. This needs a clear message and a fix (checking the key), not a retry loop.
explanation.400: A malformed request will be malformed on every retry too — the request itself needs to change, not be resent unmodified. Retrying here just delays a failure that was never going to resolve itself.

contentSections.synthesis: The dividing line is whether the exact same request, unchanged, has a real chance of succeeding on a second attempt. Transient, capacity- or timing-related failures (429, 529, most 500s) do; failures caused by something wrong with the request or credentials itself (400, 401) don't, and retrying those just delays an inevitable, identical failure.

contentSections.body: Retry only failures where the same request has a real chance of succeeding on a second try (429, 5xx) — retrying a bad API key or a malformed request just delays an identical, inevitable failure.

title: Keeping an AI-powered CLI tool's cost predictable
description: Estimating a batch job's cost before running it, defaulting to the cheapest model that does the job, and requiring confirmation before an unexpectedly expensive run — the same --yes pattern as any other consequential action.

learningObjectives.text: Estimate the token cost of a batch AI operation before running it
Design a cost-confirmation gate for a batch job that would otherwise run unexpectedly expensive

contentSections.title: The batch job that becomes a surprise bill

contentSections.body: A user runs `invtrack explain --all`, intending to generate AI summaries for every overdue invoice at once. There are 340 of them. The command runs Claude Sonnet — chosen because it was already the default for the single-invoice `explain` command — 340 times, at a cost roughly twenty times what the equivalent Haiku run would have cost, with no indication beforehand of how many calls were about to happen or roughly what they'd cost.

contentSections.scenario: invtrack explain --all is about to make one Claude call per overdue invoice, 340 of them, each a short prompt-and-response pair using claude-haiku-4-5 at roughly $0.001 per call (a realistic ballpark for a short summarization call on Haiku pricing).
contentSections.question: Roughly what would the total cost of this batch be, in dollars?
contentSections.explanation: 340 calls × ~$0.001/call ≈ $0.34 — genuinely cheap on Haiku, and a number small enough that most users would run it without a second thought if they'd been shown it upfront. The actual problem in the hook isn't that 340 AI calls are inherently expensive — it's that the command defaulted to Sonnet (roughly 20x Haiku's typical per-call cost for a task this small) purely because that was already the single-invoice default, without anyone deciding that a 340x-larger batch should reconsider that choice.

contentSections.body: The legacy CLI-tools lessons in this same domain put concrete numbers on exactly this: Haiku running 20 times a day costs roughly a cent a day; Sonnet running the same 20 times costs roughly twenty cents a day — a 20x gap that barely matters at 20 calls, and matters enormously at 340. The fix for `explain --all` is choosing the cheapest model that still does the job well for a short, low-stakes summary (Haiku, almost certainly) as the *batch* default, independent of whatever the single-invoice command's default happened to be — a default chosen for one call at a time doesn't automatically stay the right default once the same command runs hundreds of times in a row.

A model default chosen for a single call doesn't automatically stay the right default for a batch of hundreds — reconsider the cheapest-model-that-works question at batch scale specifically, not just once.

contentSections.title: The confirmation this module owes the CLI-design module

contentSections.body: Even on Haiku, someone eventually runs `invtrack explain --all` against a genuinely huge, multi-thousand-invoice historical import — a case nobody designed for, where even cheap-per-call pricing adds up to a real number. There's still no warning, no estimate, and no chance to reconsider before it just starts running.

contentSections.scenario: invtrack explain --all is about to make several thousand API calls, a cost worth pausing over even at Haiku pricing — genuinely comparable to the CLI-design module's example of a destructive, hard-to-reverse action.
contentSections.question: What's the right design, drawing on a pattern this track has already covered?

options.label: Just run it — cost isn't the kind of thing a confirmation prompt is for
Estimate the cost upfront, show it, and require confirmation above some threshold — with a --yes bypass for scripted or CI use, the same pattern used for any other consequential action
Silently cap the batch at some fixed number of invoices with no explanation

feedback.just-run: An unreviewed real cost, in real money, for an action a user might not have fully anticipated the scale of, is exactly the kind of consequence a confirmation step exists to surface before it happens, not after the bill shows up.
feedback.estimate-and-confirm: Right — this is the same --yes-bypass confirmation pattern from the CLI-design module's destructive-action lesson, applied to cost instead of data loss. A human at a terminal sees the estimate and can back out; a script that already knows what it's doing passes --yes and proceeds without being blocked.
feedback.silent-cap: An unexplained cap just produces a different kind of surprise — a user assuming the whole batch ran, discovering later that most of it silently didn't, is at least as confusing as an unexpected bill, and gives them no way to override it if the larger cost was genuinely fine with them.

contentSections.concept: **A batch AI operation above some cost threshold deserves the exact same confirm-by-default, --yes-to-bypass pattern as any other consequential action.** Estimate the cost from the item count and a per-call cost figure, show it, and let the user decide — a script that already knows what it's doing passes --yes, same as it would for a destructive delete.

contentSections.body: A batch AI operation above a real cost threshold deserves the same confirm-by-default, --yes-to-bypass pattern as any other consequential action — estimate the cost, show it, and let a human decide before it's spent.

title: Design the AI step and fallback for seven CLI ideas
description: Seven drills applying this module's filters — latency budget, streaming, caching, retry judgment, and cost estimation — to AI-powered CLI scenarios you haven't seen before.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's AI-integration filters to unfamiliar CLI scenarios at speed
Identify the specific AI-integration mistake in a real scenario, not just that something feels off

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing here expires — do them in one sitting or spread across a few.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Add an AI-powered command to a CLI tool
description: Add a real AI-backed command to a CLI tool with correct latency placement, streaming, caching, a working fallback, and predictable cost — proven against a real batch run.

learningObjectives.text: Implement an AI-backed CLI command with streaming output and a content-hash cache
Implement a graceful fallback and a cost-confirmation gate for a batch AI operation

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every filter this module covers — where the AI call belongs, streaming, caching, fallback, cost — only proves itself on a real AI-backed command doing real work. This lab adds one to a CLI tool of your own, with the Claude API doing something genuinely useful, not a toy example.

contentSections.title: An AI-powered command, built right
contentSections.brief: Pick a CLI tool from an earlier module's lab (or a new small one) and add one genuinely useful AI-backed command to it — a summarizer, an explainer, a categorizer, a suggestion generator. You'll place it correctly relative to the tool's other commands, stream its output, cache it appropriately (or explicitly justify not caching, if your use case genuinely wants variation), add a working fallback, and gate any batch use behind a cost estimate.
contentSections.deliverable: A working command with caching, streaming output and a working fallback

stages.title: Place the command and stream its output
stages.instructions: Add the AI-backed command as an explicit subcommand or flag, not folded into an existing fast/frequent command's default path. Implement it using the Claude SDK's streaming API so output appears progressively in an interactive terminal, and buffer to a single clean output when --json (or your tool's non-interactive mode) is used instead.
stages.checkpoint: The command is explicit and opt-in, streams in a terminal, and produces one clean buffered result in non-interactive/JSON mode.

stages.title: Cache it, deliberately
stages.instructions: Either implement a content-hash cache (keyed by everything the response actually depends on, stored in your tool's cache directory) with a --refresh bypass, or write down explicitly why this specific use case shouldn't cache at all, referencing what the lesson's namegen example got wrong.
stages.checkpoint: A working cache with a content-based key exists, or a stated, specific reason not to cache is written down.

stages.title: Build the fallback
stages.instructions: Make the AI call fail gracefully: isolate it so a failure doesn't crash or block any of the tool's non-AI functionality, and retry only the failure categories genuinely worth retrying (429, 5xx), not ones that won't change on a second attempt (401, 400).
stages.checkpoint: A simulated API failure produces a clear fallback message without crashing the command, and only transient-category errors trigger a retry.

stages.title: Gate the cost
stages.instructions: If your command can run in a batch (multiple items in one invocation), estimate the cost from the item count and a stated per-call estimate, and require confirmation (with a --yes bypass) above a real threshold you choose and justify.
stages.checkpoint: A batch run above your chosen threshold shows an estimated cost and requires confirmation or --yes before proceeding.

rubric.criterion: The AI call is placed correctly
rubric.meets: The command is explicit and opt-in, not folded into an existing fast, frequently-run command's default path.

rubric.criterion: Output streams for a human, buffers for a script
rubric.meets: An interactive run shows progressive output; a --json or non-interactive run emits one complete, valid result.

rubric.criterion: Caching decision is deliberate
rubric.meets: Either a working content-hash cache exists, or a specific, stated reason not to cache is documented.

rubric.criterion: A failure degrades gracefully
rubric.meets: A simulated API failure doesn't crash or block non-AI functionality, and produces a clear fallback message.

rubric.criterion: Retries are limited to transient failures
rubric.meets: 429/5xx trigger a bounded retry; 400/401 fail immediately with no retry.

rubric.criterion: Batch cost is estimated and gated
rubric.meets: A batch invocation above a stated threshold shows an estimated cost and requires confirmation or --yes.

contentSections.body: An AI feature that's fast for a human, safe when the API misbehaves, and honest about what it costs is the actual bar — not just 'it works when I demo it once, on a good connection, with one item.'

questions.from: This module — Putting AI Inside a CLI Tool
questions.prompt: invtrack overdue used to be near-instant. Why is folding an AI-generated summary into its default output the wrong call, when the same kind of AI step was fine added to import's default path?

options.label: overdue's existing latency budget (near-instant, run constantly) has almost no room for added latency; import was already multi-second and run occasionally, with real room to spare
AI calls should never be part of any command's default behavior, under any circumstances
overdue's code is technically incompatible with async API calls

questions.explanation: The deciding factor is each command's existing latency budget and run frequency — not a blanket rule about AI calls, which is exactly why the same kind of step was fine for import and wrong for overdue.

questions.from: This module — Putting AI Inside a CLI Tool
questions.prompt: Why does streaming fix the 'looks frozen' problem better than simply making the API call faster would?

options.label: The actual problem is total silence for several seconds, which reads as a hang — streaming gets the first visible token to the terminal almost immediately, regardless of the call's total duration
Streaming responses are always shorter than non-streamed ones
Streaming uses a different, faster model automatically

questions.explanation: The fix targets visible progress, not total speed — a stream shows something happening within roughly a second, which is what actually stops someone from assuming the process has hung.

questions.from: This module — Putting AI Inside a CLI Tool
questions.prompt: Why should an AI response cache be keyed by a hash of the actual input content, not by an identifier like an invoice ID?

options.label: An ID-based key keeps serving a stale answer after the underlying data changes; a content-hash key automatically misses (and refreshes) the moment anything the answer depends on actually changes
Hashing is required by the Claude API's terms of service
IDs are slower to look up than hashes in a filesystem cache

questions.explanation: A content hash naturally invalidates itself the instant something the response could depend on changes — an ID doesn't, because the ID can stay the same while the underlying data it points to changes underneath it.

questions.from: This module — Putting AI Inside a CLI Tool
questions.prompt: Of 429, 500, 529, 401 and 400, which should trigger an automatic retry?

options.label: 429, 500 and 529 — transient, capacity- or timing-related failures where the same request has a real chance of succeeding shortly after
All five — every failed API call should be retried automatically
401 and 400 — anything involving the request's validity should be retried until it succeeds

questions.explanation: 401 and 400 reflect something wrong with the credentials or the request itself, which won't change between identical attempts — retrying those just delays an inevitable, identical failure, unlike the genuinely transient categories.

questions.from: The previous module — Packaging and Distribution
questions.prompt: A one-line rename of a subcommand, with no alias kept for the old name, breaks every script that called it. What semver bump does this actually require?

options.label: MAJOR — anything that breaks existing usage, regardless of how small the code change was
PATCH — it's a small, one-line change
MINOR — it adds a new command name

questions.explanation: Semver measures compatibility, not effort — a tiny change that breaks existing callers is MAJOR.

questions.from: The previous module — Packaging and Distribution
questions.prompt: Why does a package with no files field or .npmignore often ship far more than a user's install actually needs?

options.label: npm's default is inclusive — everything not on a small built-in ignore list ships, unless something explicitly scopes it down
npm pads small packages with extra files to meet a minimum size
This only happens if the bin field is misconfigured

questions.explanation: Without an explicit files allowlist, npm ships everything in the project directory by default, minus a small built-in ignore list.

questions.from: The previous module — Packaging and Distribution
questions.prompt: For a CLI tool distributed exclusively via npm, what's the strongest argument against building bespoke auto-update logic?

options.label: npm's own update path already solves the problem, and bespoke logic adds a second, less-scrutinized delivery surface for no real benefit
Users never want their CLI tools updated automatically
Auto-update is technically impossible to implement in Node.js

questions.explanation: The existing distribution channel already solves the problem, making bespoke update logic redundant risk for a benefit that already exists for free.

questions.from: The previous module — Packaging and Distribution
questions.prompt: Why does a filename-casing bug (Utils.js imported, utils.js on disk) pass locally on macOS but fail in a Linux CI runner?

options.label: macOS's default filesystem is case-insensitive and tolerates the mismatch; Linux's is case-sensitive and treats them as two different, unrelated names
This indicates a CI configuration bug, since the exact same code passed locally
Node.js resolves imports differently on each OS by design

questions.explanation: A case-insensitive local filesystem hides a real bug that a case-sensitive one (like Linux, common in CI) correctly surfaces.

questions.from: Three or more modules back — State, Config and Secrets
questions.prompt: What's the actual reason an environment variable is safer than a config file for a credential?

options.label: It doesn't sit in a file that gets backed up, synced, or committed to a dotfiles repo the way a config file does
Operating systems automatically encrypt environment variables at rest
Environment variables can only be read by the process that set them

questions.explanation: Env vars aren't automatically encrypted — the real advantage is structural, not cryptographic.

questions.from: Three or more modules back — State, Config and Secrets
questions.prompt: When invtrack's keychain integration fails inside a headless CI container, what's the right response?

options.label: Fall back to an env var or restricted-permission file, and say so explicitly, once, on stderr
Crash immediately with the raw native-module error
Silently write the credential in plaintext with no notice

questions.explanation: The explicit, once-announced fallback keeps the tool working and the security-posture change visible — the same shape this module reused for AI-call failures degrading to a clear fallback rather than crashing.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint — that's the design, not a failure.
